subject: Using pcount() and ranef() only to correct for imperfect detection

messages.author: a1d454f60d33ee10
messages.subject: Using pcount() and ranef() only to correct for imperfect detection
parts:
Hello.

I am interested in size effects of environmental variables in species abundance. However, I'm aware that detection probabilities may not be constant, but dependent on detection variables. Therefore I'm using Pcount models and the function ranef() to correct and estimate abundance. As a next step I intend to use this estimative as response variable in a multiple regression and hierarchical partitioning to acces size effects of environmental variables on species abundance. Does it makes sense? Or Should I add the environmental variables as an occupancy variable to estimate abundance? This second scenario looks redundant to me because I would estimate abundance based on environmental variables and then, would try to correlate such data to this variables. It might be right because I'm only interested in size effects. Does any of this situations makes any sense? Or should I move on to a model selection approach, which does not gives me accurate variable size effects?

Cheers! Rodolfo.

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: [unmarked] Using pcount() and ranef() only to correct for imperfect detection
parts:
Dear Rodolfo,

 

Go the second way ! That way, you do all at once in a single model and you know what you’re doing. Ad hoc composite analyses like the first one have lots of risks in my opinion of doing things which are suboptimal, to say the least.

 

A binomial mixture model (that’s the one fit using function pcount --- remember not to call a model by the name of the function or the software used to fit it) gives you all at once, in a statistical rigorous way without any ad-hockery.

 

You have N ~ Poisson(lambda) as the model for the latent abundance N and C ~ Binomial (N, p) as your measurement error model for the observed data C and you can add covariates in either process as you are interested in them and as they’re available in a GLM-way via a link function. Note that you have two types of abundance in this model (and in reality, too): the realized abundance at a site (N) and the expected abundance (lambda). This has been discussed in this list before (or in the sister list, HMecology).

 

To gauge the relationship between abundance and covariates you will not normally look at the estimated N’s for your surveyed sites (i.e., at the realized abundance) but at the expected abundance at any site given the value of some covariates. Hence, use one the predict functions and predict expected abundance for a range of values for the covariates and then plot this relationship: that shows you how covariates affect (expected) abundance.

 

If you want to compare the effect sizes of different covariates I am not so sure. I presume you could fit all covariates after scaling them to make them comparable and then directly compare their coefficient estimates. An alternative might be to fit the model bayesianly (e.g., in BUGS software --- then it’s clearly no longer “the pcount model”) and use ideas expressed in the paper by Qian and Shen, Ecology, 2007 (And Gelman 2005 before), to compare effect sizes of explanatory variables.  Another alternative to compare the magnitude of effects of different environmental covariates, which I think is very interesting, has been described by Beale et al. (see here http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12174/abstract). They essentially do a sensitivity analysis by disturbing the value of each covariate by a constant amount and then observe which covariate, when such noise is added, leads to the greatest change in the estimated abundance. This is especially useful if you have complex covariate relationships, e.g., polynomials, interactions, or splines.

 

Best regards  --- Marc
